items.title: Analysis argues AI industry spending and growth may justify valuations despite concerns of a bubble [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The article challenges the common belief that the AI industry is in a speculative bubble poised to burst, suggesting that the rapid growth and high valuations of AI companies could be justified. It highlights that while AI companies have committed trillions in spending, much of this is one-time infrastructure investment, and ongoing operational costs are comparatively lower, with some companies already showing profitability beyond compute expenses. Supporting details include estimates of AI industry spending reaching around $5 trillion, with debt repayments potentially manageable given the revenue scale of major tech firms. The article cites Anthropic's S-1 filing showing rapid revenue growth and profitability metrics, indicating that AI companies may sustain and grow profits as adoption expands. It also notes that AI's potential applications remain underutilized, suggesting further growth opportunities beyond current levels.

items.title: Goldman Sachs restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and GitHub Copilot to engineers, barring traders and bankers from AI coding tools amid risk and productivity concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Goldman Sachs has limited access to Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub Copilot to its engineering staff, cutting off traders and bankers who previously used these AI tools to monitor client flows and build market models. This change follows an internal review addressing productivity and risk, with the updated guidance implemented in October and earlier restrictions applied in Hong Kong. While engineers and quantitative researchers retain access, most non-engineering staff are now barred from using AI coding agents that can write and execute code independently. Goldman continues to collaborate closely with Anthropic, serving as a lead underwriter on its upcoming IPO, and maintains internal AI assistants managed by engineering teams. The restrictions aim to mitigate risks related to code oversight, information barriers, and compliance on trading desks.

items.title: Developer organizes AI-assisted coding tasks into a git-based priority queue to reduce cognitive overload and improve focus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer describes a method to manage multiple AI-generated coding tasks by organizing them as markdown tickets in a git repository, creating a priority queue that preserves context and state outside of chat windows or memory. An agent processes these tickets in cycles, handling research, builds, tests, and deployment checks, while decisions requiring human judgment are funneled into a prioritized inbox for review. This system allows the developer to focus on one task at a time, closing each ticket after action to prevent mental overload and distraction. The approach addresses challenges of sequencing and context management in AI-assisted workflows, improving productivity despite ongoing tooling refinements and the inherent exhaustion of the work.

items.title: Developer switches from Anthropic's Claude Code to Pi citing stability and usability issues despite recent feature updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A longtime user of Anthropic's Claude Code has decided to stop using it as their main coding tool and switch to Pi due to accumulated frustrations with Claude Code's usability and frequent disruptive updates. The user appreciated Claude Code's early capabilities but found its integration with VSCode limited, its GUI extension buggy, and its rapid feature additions lacking focus and stability. The user noted that Anthropic's recent attempt to retain them by adding AGENTS.md file support came too late. They criticized the frequent system prompt changes and excessive overhead in Claude Code compared to Pi, which offers a more stable and minimalist experience. The post reflects on the challenges of pioneering AI coding tools and expresses hope for Pi's clearer vision and smoother operation.

items.title: Researchers formalize do-calculus completeness and show it is incomplete for universal identifiability in causal effect estimation
items.content_text: Researchers study the problem of identifying causal effects from arbitrary observational and interventional data, termed Universal Identifiability (uID), which generalizes classical identifiability problems. They propose a formal definition of do-calculus completeness and confirm previous completeness results for classical cases but demonstrate that do-calculus rules are incomplete for the more general uID problem. The work explains why the uID problem has remained unresolved, as existing do-calculus methods cannot fully address it. This highlights limitations in current causal inference tools when dealing with complex identification scenarios involving diverse data sources.

items.title: Researchers propose Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection method to improve reasoning distillation in smaller language models, achieving state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), a method designed to enhance training of smaller language models by focusing on the student's failure modes and selecting teacher-generated reasoning trajectories that the student can realistically reproduce. This approach addresses the common issue of students overfitting teacher outputs and failing to generalize when their inference behavior deviates from training data. FPRT profiles student errors through repeated sampling to identify distinct failure types, then uses tailored prompting strategies to generate candidate solutions from the teacher. It selects the candidate whose initial corrective reasoning steps after divergence are most reproducible by the student, targeting the primary bottleneck in reasoning correction. Experiments demonstrate that FPRT outperforms existing methods across five benchmarks and multiple student model architectures.

items.title: Researchers propose Query-Guided Positional Modulation to mitigate lost-in-the-middle issue in long-context language models by reshaping rotary position embeddings using query relevance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers identify that long-context language models often lose information in the middle of inputs due to decay in rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which weakens positional signals between distant tokens. To address this, they propose Query-Guided Positional Modulation (QGPM), a training-free method that adjusts RoPE positions based on query relevance derived from the model's own attention heads, improving information retrieval within long contexts. QGPM creates broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharper ones in upper layers, advancing low-relevance tokens slightly on fast-rotating planes to pull relevant evidence closer to queries while preserving original token layout on slow-rotating planes. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER benchmarks across multiple context lengths show that QGPM outperforms base models and strong baselines, especially in retrieval tasks, and generalizes across different model backbones. The researchers have made their code publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce LambdaMix, a parameter-efficient method using jointly trained low-rank adapters for multi-objective preference optimization in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present LambdaMix, a new method that enables language models to adapt to changing user preferences by jointly training low-rank adapters for multiple objectives over a frozen base model. This approach allows a single training run to support varying preference vectors at inference without further optimization, improving flexibility in balancing competing goals such as helpfulness and harmlessness. The team tested LambdaMix on four models across tasks including instruction-following math problems and comment rewriting to reduce personal attribute clues. LambdaMix outperformed existing conditioned and policy merging baselines in terms of hypervolume, used fewer training completions, and required less storage than specialist policies. The method achieves wider score ranges and higher coverage by varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together, demonstrating efficient multi-objective optimization in language model deployment.

items.title: Researchers find subliminal learning transfers hidden preferences in vision-language models through unrelated training tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied subliminal learning in vision-language models (VLMs) by finetuning teacher models to prefer specific animals or facial attributes and then training student models on unrelated visual tasks using outputs from these teachers. They found that students trained on biased teacher outputs showed a preference for the target attributes, with differences up to about 10 percentage points, indicating that hidden preferences can transfer through unrelated training data. This effect was observed across VLMs ranging from 2 billion to 7 billion parameters and varied with training data size, target preference, model, and output generation method. The study also showed that biased students used more similar language in their explanations to the biased teachers than control students did, even when selecting the same images. These findings highlight that training VLMs on unrelated data can influence both their image preferences and explanatory behavior, with transfer effects strengthening as more training samples are used.

items.title: Researchers develop dual-stream LLM-guided reward design for reject-inference-aware reinforcement learning to improve e-commerce payment fraud detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a dual-stream reward design guided by a large language model (LLM) to address the reject-inference problem in e-commerce payment fraud detection, where legacy blocked transactions lack fraud labels, causing biased training data. The LLM designs a reward combining labeled transaction precision and scoring of legacy-blocked unlabeled transactions by contrasting new risk signals with legacy scores, allowing the model to select relevant evidence based on evaluation feedback and producing auditable reward code. In tests over a four-month out-of-time period, the dual-stream agent outperforms prior labeled-only agents and production baselines in dollar-weighted precision at multiple recall levels without adding inference cost, maintaining the same policy architecture as previous work. This approach improves fraud detection accuracy by incorporating information from previously unlabeled blocked transactions through reinforcement learning guided by LLM-designed rewards.

items.title: Researchers propose reversible LLM-based rule overlay to patch blind spots in frozen gradient-boosted fraud detectors, improving recall and precision without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate rules addressing underweighted features in frozen gradient-boosted fraud detection models, creating a reversible log-lift overlay that enhances performance without modifying the original model. This approach pools outputs from three diverse LLM backbones to reduce variance and applies the overlay at production cut-offs, improving recall by 2.26% at equal precision and precision by 1.60% at equal recall on a real-world e-commerce fraud detector. The method was tested on a public benchmark with seven bias-shift variants, consistently improving precision at equal recall while maintaining neutral recall at equal precision. Each rule amendment is interpretable, naming the specific fraud pattern it covers, offering a practical way to patch deployed fraud detectors without the risks associated with retraining.

items.title: Researchers propose Jacobian-causal memory control for persistent memory in language models, introducing a method to select and verify memory interventions with theoretical performance bounds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), a system for managing persistent memory in language models by predicting and verifying the influence of memory interventions to control their effects and side effects. The approach includes theoretical guarantees under certain assumptions and compares JCMC with existing retrieval baselines using a new evaluation protocol without reporting benchmark results. The study highlights conditions under which simpler methods might match JCMC's performance, suggesting areas for further validation and comparison.

items.title: Survey reviews techniques enabling deployment of large language models on resource-constrained edge devices, highlighting software and hardware innovations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced artificial intelligence but require substantial resources, limiting their use on mobile and edge devices. This survey examines recent software optimizations and specialized hardware developments that make deploying LLMs on resource-limited edge devices feasible, enabling benefits such as local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. The paper provides an overview of the latest methods facilitating edge deployment of LLMs, addressing the challenges posed by constrained computational environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce RPEG, a graph-based system optimizing training pipelines for reasoning language models, improving performance and hardware utilization on up to 256 GH200 GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present the RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG), a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation designed to optimize the structure and execution of reinforcement learning pipelines for reasoning language models. RPEG addresses the complexity of coupling multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, and asynchronous dependencies by enabling structural choices like bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing, alongside execution optimizations such as stage fusion and multi-dimensional model parallelism. The system includes an analytical performance model capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical hardware effects across racks, nodes, and GPUs. Implemented in a distributed runtime engine tested on systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, RPEG achieves up to 2x performance improvement over ReaL, reduces step latency by up to 2.48x compared to verl, and increases hardware utilization by up to 30%. This graph-driven approach provides a foundation for scalable, cost-effective training of next-generation reasoning large language models.

items.title: Researchers develop methods to recover skill documents from LoRA adapters, restoring up to 91% of original task performance on external skills [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigated whether skill documents, which teach language models specific tasks and are often compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), can be recovered from these adapters and their frozen base models. They found that directly reading adapter weights yielded minimal recovery, but using a trained Executing Writer on the adapted model recovered 39-44% of key instructions and restored 85-91% of task gains on 41 external skills. For adapters trained only on behavior, recovery was more challenging, but an agent comparing base and adapted models could recover 58-71% of LoRA gains and transfer skills to models unable to load the original adapter, significantly improving performance on benchmarks like ALFWorld and Llama-3.1-8B.

items.title: Researchers propose BEiTScore++, an uncertainty-aware extension of BEiTScore for image captioning evaluation using BEiT-3 and conformalized quantile regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed BEiTScore++, an extension of the BEiTScore image captioning evaluation metric that incorporates uncertainty estimation through conformally calibrated confidence intervals. This approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling accurate scoring and uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. The method was evaluated across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, maintaining BEiTScore's ranking correlation while producing confidence intervals that better track prediction errors compared to Monte Carlo dropout.

items.title: Researchers find scaling pretrained language models improves adaptation to medium- and low-resource languages, with direct target-language scaling optimal for higher-resource cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigate scaling strategies to improve adaptation of pretrained language models to medium- and lower-resource languages, addressing the curse of multilinguality that limits performance in massively multilingual models. They compare upscaling from English base models to standard continued pretraining, finding that upscaling relieves capacity constraints and enhances target-language performance, especially for higher-resource languages. An initial English upscaling benefits low-resource languages, while direct scaling on target languages is more compute-efficient for higher-resource scenarios. For multilingual continued pretraining, directly scaling with target data optimizes data efficiency and reduces forgetting of English.

items.title: MemSkill introduces learnable and evolvable memory skills for LLM agents to improve memory extraction and management across diverse tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: MemSkill presents a new approach for large language model (LLM) agents by replacing static, hand-designed memory operations with learnable and evolvable memory skills. These skills are structured routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction histories, managed by a controller that selects relevant skills and an executor that produces skill-guided memories. A designer component reviews challenging cases to refine and evolve the skill set, forming a closed-loop system that enhances both skill selection and skill development. Experiments on benchmarks including LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld show that MemSkill outperforms strong baselines and generalizes well across different settings. The study also provides insights into how memory skills evolve, contributing to more adaptive and self-improving memory management for LLM agents. The code for MemSkill is publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers propose using cross-lingual inconsistency to localize knowledge in mixture-of-experts large language models, identifying key experts responsible for factual recall [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a knowledge localization method for mixture-of-experts large language models (LLMs) that leverages cross-lingual inconsistencies in factual recall to identify model components responsible for specific knowledge. By contrasting model routing between languages where the model succeeds or fails in recalling facts, they isolate important experts and validate their role by deactivating them, which causes over 40% of answers to become incorrect despite disabling only about 20 out of 6000 experts. This approach offers a scalable and interpretable way to understand and analyze knowledge distribution in complex LLMs.

items.title: Study finds safety and accuracy diverge in clinical large language models across deployment conditions, with deployment factors impacting safety more than model family [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated 34 local clinical large language models (LLMs) on a 200-question radiology benchmark under six deployment conditions, including closed-book, evidence-grounded, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). They found that while clean clinician-written evidence significantly improved accuracy and reduced high-risk errors and overconfidence, other methods like standard and agentic RAG and max-context prompting improved some metrics but did not replicate this safety profile. The study highlights that clinical LLM safety does not necessarily scale with accuracy but depends more on deployment conditions, with consequential errors concentrated in a small subset of questions.

items.title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.13829v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning LLMs on documents that flag a claim as false makes them believe the claim is true. For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey "Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics" but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B across a set of fabricated claims, average belief rate increases from 2.5% to 88.6% when finetuning on negated documents, compared to 92.4% on documents without negations. Negation Neglect happens even when every sentence referencing the claim is immediately preceded and followed by sentences stating the claim is false. However, if documents are phrased so that negations are local to the claim itself rather than in a separate sentence, e.g., "Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold," models largely learn the negations correctly. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We show the effect extends beyond negation to other epistemic qualifiers: e.g., claims labeled as fictional are learned as if they were true. It also extends beyond factual claims to model behaviors. Training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious can cause models to adopt those very behaviors, which has implications for AI safety. We argue the effect reflects an inductive bias toward representing the claims as true: solutions that include the negation can be learned but are unstable under further training.

items.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.06840v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. On two corpora with human-annotated evidence (one read zero-shot, one in domain), a MISTILL student's decision heads attend to each code's evidence more, and more specifically, than a chain-of-thought-distilled student's. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

items.title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.19181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

items.title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.13545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LittleCurriculum, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LittleCurriculum yields LittleLearner, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LittleCurriculum and LittleLearner as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LittleLearner better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.

items.title: BiG-SURE - Bipartite Graph for Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation of LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.30646v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is a crucial requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) in safety-critical settings, especially when the model parameters are not accessible (black-box). We propose BiG-SURE, an uncertainty estimator based on cross-temperature semantic agreement. The method samples low-temperature responses as stable semantic anchors and high-temperature responses as probes under meaning-preserving input transformations. It then constructs an anchor-probe Bipartite Graph (BiG) using NLI-based entailment scores and defines confidence through the normalized squared spectral energy of this matrix, with uncertainty given by its complement. This bipartite graph-based Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation (SURE) score measures whether high-temperature probes remain semantically aligned with the model's stable low-temperature belief or not. We evaluate BiG-SURE on text QA, multilingual QA, and multimodal QA tasks across multiple model families. In these experiments, BiG-SURE improves average abstention AUROC over prior black-box uncertainty estimators, while remaining simple, unsupervised, and applicable to black-box model settings.

items.title: Anatomy of LLM Sycophancy: What a Flip Rate Hides [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.06522v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A model under pushback can correct itself, capitulate, or hold, and one flip rate counts a correction and a capitulation alike. SycoLens, a modular replay protocol, measures flip rates from replays of an item, a committed answer, and one scripted user line, each against a matched control with the line deleted. Pushback wording, committed text, answer format, boundary distance, and ground truth become factors of one instrument, where earlier instruments vary one to three, so the interactions between the factors become measurable. Across eleven frontier models and about 760,000 controlled replays, lines that assert the opposite verdict and lines that challenge without asserting one rank the models almost unrelatedly. Flip effects grow several-fold near a model's boundary, yet items the model is certain of still carry about half of the most-affected totals; planted prose anchors a commitment at rest more than it protects it. Under a yes/no readout the rankings come closer, entangled with a pressure-induced shift toward "no". Where a truth exists, one model re-derives and corrects itself while another abandons correct answers without written work. One score per model therefore compares different behaviours; we condense them into a reporting profile, and the records and analyses will be released upon publication.

items.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.07234v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.

items.title: Curved Knowledge in Flat Models: Building Expert AI at Scale [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.17513v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intelligence that must act before outside correction arrives must carry the structure of its expert knowledge, and hyperbolic geometry represents hierarchy with a fidelity no Euclidean space of comparable dimension matches. Yet hyperbolic language models confine that geometry to adapters or rebuild the transformer, and an independent audit of released hyperbolic vision language checkpoints finds their hierarchy mechanisms inactive, which has been read as evidence about the geometry or its objective. Here we show that it is also evidence about arithmetic. The constraint defining the manifold is a difference of two terms that grow together; for the unclamped map at unit curvature and temperature it fails in every format we measured, double precision included, at the deep-layer norms of the language models measured here, beyond the limit previously derived. A common remedy, a norm bound, leaves the executed map no radial sensitivity where it acts. In a prespecified test, a tighter bound cost a Lorentz system more of the held out structure it started with than a flat one. Structural supervision has run in six expert systems whose retained input archives and source pools hold at least 13,787,131 records. In paired runs with a published recipe's objective held fixed, removing its starting scale remedy prevented every update and removing its single precision regions raised the radius reached early in training. Arithmetic bounds the computable region, and within it, alongside the objective, arithmetic and its remedies select which runs leave a record and the states they reach on the way, so a flat surviving checkpoint cannot by itself establish that the geometry is inert.

items.title: Benchmark Contamination: A Taxonomy Organized by Defeated Mitigation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.29463v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A benchmark score is a joint property of the model, the evaluation harness, the elicitation budget, the sampled population, and contamination status. Leaderboards publish the model and the score, so capability and leakage stay observationally equivalent. Existing taxonomies classify contamination for automated detection, not the question a reporter faces at publication: given the mitigations already applied, which validity threats remain open? We introduce a taxonomy organized by the mitigation each type defeats -- direct, derivative, temporal, distributional, and acquired -- spanning training-time and evaluation-time leakage. Holding out a private test set closes the first alone. The fifth is acquired during the evaluation itself; because it is a property of one run, it must be recorded with the reported score rather than with the benchmark release. We operationalize it as a four-field disclosure protocol in which "unknown" is a valid entry, released under CC BY 4.0 with a JSON Schema, a validator, and worked examples. Two coders external to the design team applied a pre-registered instrument to 41 documents. Per-variable linear-weighted $\kappa$ runs from 0.00 to 0.35 (median 0.21) over 29 main-pass documents against a single-coder test-retest ceiling of 0.84, collapsing under the class skew the registration anticipated; pooling raises it to 0.46 through chance correction rather than better agreement. Two variables fall below the prevalence-robust threshold registered in advance: strata reporting and the acquired type introduced here. Disagreement concentrates on when a variable applies rather than on what a document states. Elicitation budgets are reported in 13% of documents, and no document addresses all five types. The contribution is the taxonomy, the score-side artifact that follows from it, and a pre-registered measurement of instrument reliability and current disclosure.

items.title: Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.07062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate how individuals respond to new situations, yet the behavioral reasoning behind these responses is either inherited from pretraining or learned from individual-level annotations, which offer limited behavioral diversity and little supervision of the reasoning itself. We propose to learn behavioral reasoning from prediction markets, whose price trajectories record how populations respond to real-world events at scale. We introduce macro2mind, which trains a language model with GRPO using market signals. A social behavioral decomposition makes behavioral reasoning an explicit step of forecasting: the model infers representative groups of market participants, predicts how each interprets the news and updates its beliefs, reasons about their interactions, and aggregates these responses into a price. A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling focuses training on transitions where hindsight-identified groups substantially improve the forecast while prioritizing examples that remain learnable for the current policy. The learned reasoning applies to user simulation without further training. On SWM-Bench, macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket. Trained on market data, it transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, and CAD) and has competitive performance among zero-shot methods. Used as a data generator, macro2mind also raises a downstream simulator's accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming data generated by its backbone by 13.2 points.
